result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_chordal()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if an undirected graph is chordal (triangulated). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L22152-L22210){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_chordal() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is chordal](/assets/graphs/is-chordal.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a square A, B, C, D with the diagonal A to C, which splits it into two triangles, so every cycle of four or more nodes has a chord and is_chordal() returns True. Right: the square without the diagonal; the cycle A, B, C, D (shown in the accent color) has no chord, so is_chordal() returns False." width="100%"} A graph is chordal when every cycle of four or more nodes has a *chord*, an edge joining two nodes of the cycle that are not consecutive on it; equivalently, it has no induced cycle longer than a triangle. Trees, complete graphs, interval graphs and k-trees are all chordal. Chordal graphs are where many hard problems become easy: maximum cliques, optimal colorings and tree decompositions can all be read off a perfect elimination ordering, which is why sparse matrix factorization, Bayesian network inference (junction trees) and phylogenetics rely on them. Parallel edges count once and self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph is chordal. Graphs with at most three nodes always are. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Maximum cardinality search (Tarjan and Yannakakis, 1984) numbers the nodes one at a time, always picking the node with the most numbered neighbors; the graph is chordal exactly when, for every node, its previously numbered neighbors form a clique, in which case the reverse order is a perfect elimination ordering. Results match NetworkX's `is_chordal`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A square is the smallest graph that is not chordal; adding a diagonal makes it chordal: ::: {#80f7c018 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec square = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) square.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")]) before = square.is_chordal() square.add_edge("A", "C") before, square.is_chordal() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (False, True) ``` ::: :::
